analysis.reason: The paper quantifies neutrino point-source and stacking detectability of X-ray-bright Seyfert coronae with a global telescope network, which is relevant to compact-object neutrino observations but is not central to FRB, supernova-engine, or jet-breakout work.
analysis.result: In all three scenarios the Circinus Galaxy is by far the brightest southern Seyfert in both neutrinos and MeV $\gamma$-rays. If Seyferts supply the diffuse astrophysical neutrino flux up to ${\sim}100\,\mathrm{TeV}$ and Circinus has at least the population-average neutrino luminosity, the IceCube--Baikal-GVD--KM3NeT/ARCA--P-ONE network reaches $5\sigma$ on Circinus by 2038 at the latest; Appendix C gives ${\sim}6.1\sigma$ (NGC 1068-like, $5\sigma$ in 2033) and ${\sim}6.2\sigma$ (average, $5\sigma$ in 2038) by 2040. The scenarios are $(P_{\mathrm{CR}}/P_{\mathrm{th}},\eta)=(0.5,56)$ (NGC 1068-like), $(0.01,1)$ (average), and $(0.5,1)$ (optimistic), with $\eta=B^{2}/\delta B^{2}$. Using NGC 1068 parameters for every source exceeds the TeV diffuse flux by $3.8\sigma$; fitting the flux below ${\sim}100\,\mathrm{TeV}$ instead requires $P_{\mathrm{CR}}/P_{\mathrm{th}}\lesssim 0.05$ and $\eta\lesssim 10$ for most sources. Other nearby Seyferts remain hard to detect individually. For $F_X\ge 10^{-11}\,\mathrm{erg}\,\mathrm{cm}^{-2}\,\mathrm{s}^{-1}$, the 2040 optimal stack is $N_{\mathrm{src}}\sim 50$--$70$ with Circinus and ${\sim}100$--$130$ without it.
analysis.problem: Can X-ray-bright Seyfert coronae be discovered as individual neutrino point sources, or only by X-ray-informed stacking, if a hidden coronal origin like NGC 1068 accounts for the diffuse astrophysical neutrino flux without accompanying TeV $\gamma$-rays?
analysis.method: Protons are stochastically accelerated in a magnetized corona of size $R_c=r_c R_S$ with $R_S=2GM_{\mathrm{BH}}/c^{2}$, and neutrinos come from photohadronic interactions on coronal X-rays plus hadronuclear interactions; $\gamma$-rays are $\gamma\gamma$-absorbed and emerge mainly at MeV energies. Forecasts use PLE$\nu$M and Asimov data in bins of $\log\hat{E}$ and $\Delta\Psi^{2}=|\hat{\Omega}-\Omega_{\mathrm{src}}|^{2}$, with $\lambda_{ij}(\boldsymbol{\theta})=\lambda_{ij}^{\mathrm{astro}}+\lambda_{ij}^{\mathrm{atm}}$ and $\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{tot}}=\prod_k\mathcal{L}_k$. Each of IceCube, Baikal-GVD, KM3NeT/ARCA, and P-ONE is assigned $1\,\mathrm{km}^{3}$; water detectors are given IceCube-like effective area but better angular resolution for $E_{\nu}\gtrsim 10\,\mathrm{TeV}$ because of the longer Cherenkov-photon scattering length.
assumptions: Water-based neutrino telescopes are expected to achieve better angular resolution than IceCube at high neutrino energies because Cherenkov photons have a longer scattering length.
limits: The optimistic scenario overestimates the neutrino production efficiency of all three sources in the IceCube comparison of NGC 1194, CGCG 164-019, and NGC 7212.

IV.3 Results: “the Circinus Galaxy is expected to be by far the brightest Seyfert galaxy”
IV.3 Results: “This suggests that the optimistic scenario overestimates the neutrino production efficiency of all three sources.”
VI Conclusions: “provided that the Seyfert population is responsible for the diffuse astrophysical neutrino flux”
III Neutrino telescope network: “Due to the longer scattering length of Cherenkov photons in water”
Appendix A Angular resolution function of KM3NeT/ARCA: “a narrower angular resolution function results in a neutrino being reconstructed closer”
analysis.research_progress: The incremental result is a network forecast rather than a new detection: under the diffuse-flux normalization, Circinus is the only robust southern point source, reaching $5\sigma$ by 2038, while stacking about $N_{\mathrm{src}}\sim 100$ X-ray-selected Seyferts saturates sensitivity. Spectral peaks are ${\sim}1\,\mathrm{TeV}$ in the NGC 1068-like case and ${\sim}10\,\mathrm{TeV}$ in the average case, and MeV $\gamma$-ray observations can separate the three $(P_{\mathrm{CR}}/P_{\mathrm{th}},\eta)$ scenarios.

The light green dashed and solid lines correspond to the neutrino and $\gamma$ -ray spectra for $P_{\mathrm{CR}}/P_{\mathrm{th}}=0.5$ and $\eta=1$. For each source, the $\gamma$ -ray spectrum measured by Fermi-LAT [ 38 ] is shown for comparison, with downward-pointing arrows indicating $95\hskip 1.0pt\%$ upper limits. In addition, the sensitivity of COMPTEL [ 52 ] is shown for its total lifetime of ${\sim}\hskip 1.0pt9\,\mathrm{years}$, while the sensitivity curves of COSI [ 55 ], AMEGO-X [ 18 ], and newASTROGAM [ 16 ] are shown for an observation time of $3\,\mathrm{years}$.

analysis.reason: This Swift-XRT population study separates early–narrow and late–wide GRB X-ray flares and tests prolonged accretion against external-shock variability, directly constraining compact-object central engines and relativistic outflows.
analysis.result: A rest-frame GMM of $(t_{\rm pk},w)$ yields two populations: early–narrow (~80%, $\langle t_{\rm pk}\rangle\simeq10^{2}\,{\rm s}$, $w/t_{\rm pk}\lesssim1$; center $\log_{10}(t_{\rm pk},w)=(1.97,1.85)$) and late–wide (~20%, $\langle t_{\rm pk}\rangle\simeq10^{3.5}\,{\rm s}$, $w/t_{\rm pk}\gtrsim2$; center $(3.49,3.80)$). Their mean energies are consistent, $\langle\log_{10}(E_{\rm iso,f,rest})\rangle=51.13\pm0.10$ versus $50.66\pm0.20$ (K–S $p=0.22$). Early–narrow flares follow $L_{\rm avg,f,rest}\propto t_{\rm pk,rest}^{-1.74^{+0.24}_{-0.24}}$, while late–wide flares give $-0.19^{+1.01}_{-0.93}$; the combined slope is $-1.60^{+0.12}_{-0.12}$, shallower than $L_{\rm pk}\propto t_{\rm pk}^{-3}$. The global fit $\log w_{\rm rest}=\alpha+\beta\log t_{\rm pk,rest}$ has $\beta=1.21^{+0.06}_{-0.06}$, but only early–narrow flares are significant ($\beta=1.04^{+0.12}_{-0.13}$, $w/t_{\rm pk}\sim0.76$ versus $\sim2.04$). Waiting times are $\sim76\,{\rm s}$ versus $\sim2950\,{\rm s}$.
analysis.reading_entry: IV.4 Implications for accretion-powered central engine models
analysis.problem: The origin of GRB X-ray flares is unresolved: they may be prolonged central-engine activity or external-shock variability, and it is unclear whether one temporal scaling describes all flares.
analysis.method: Light curves from 100 redshift-known Swift-BAT GRBs (89 fitted; 61 with flares) are modeled with asymmetric Norris profiles. Rest-frame $t_{\rm pk}$, $w$, asymmetry, and $E_{\rm iso,f}$ adopt flat $\Lambda$CDM with $\Omega_{\rm m}=0.286$ and $H_0=70\,{\rm km\,s^{-1}\,Mpc^{-1}}$. A multivariate GMM classifies $(t_{\rm pk},w)$; K–S, Spearman, and Bayesian regression test relations. Luminosity is $L_{\rm avg,f,rest}=E_{\rm iso,f,rest}/w_{\rm rest}$, and accretion timing is compared with $t_{\rm visc}\sim\alpha^{-1}(H/R)^{-2}\Omega_K^{-1}$.
assumptions: Fallback material circularizes and then accretes on the viscous time $t_{\rm visc}\sim\alpha^{-1}(H/R)^{-2}\Omega_K^{-1}$.
limits: Broad flares can be absorbed into empirical power-law afterglow segments, and 11 bursts with extremely large fitted widths were excluded.

analysis.research_progress: The global $w$–$t_{\rm pk}$ relation is not universal: early–narrow flares retain $w/t_{\rm pk}\sim0.76$ and fade as $L_{\rm avg,f,rest}\propto t_{\rm pk,rest}^{-1.74}$, whereas late–wide flares have $w/t_{\rm pk}\sim2.04$, $\sim2950\,{\rm s}$ waiting times, and no significant luminosity decline. The slope is shallower than hyperaccretion $L\propto t^{-3}$, while fallback and viscous times of tens to $\sim10^{3}\,{\rm s}$ favor prolonged accretion over a pure time shift or one external-shock scaling.

figures.caption: Figure 5: Left: Relation between the average flare luminosity, $L_{\rm avg,f,rest}=E_{\rm iso,f,rest}/w_{\rm rest}$, and the rest-frame flare peak time, $t_{\rm pk,rest}$, for the early–narrow (purple) and late–wide (green) flare populations. The dashed lines show the median Bayesian linear regression obtained with LinMix, while the faint lines represent random posterior realizations of the fitted relation. The quoted slopes correspond to the median posterior values with their 68% credible intervals. A statistically significant anti-correlation is found for the early–narrow flares, whereas no significant trend is detected for the late–wide population. Because the average flare luminosity is not identical to the instantaneous jet luminosity, this relation provides only an indirect comparison with the luminosity evolution predicted by accretion-powered central-engine models. Right: Average flare luminosity as a function of rest-frame peak time for the combined flare sample (Cluster 0 + Cluster 1; grey circles), together with the geometric mean luminosities in logarithmic bins of peak time (open squares), following Margutti et al. [37]. The horizontal error bars on the binned measurements represent the 16th–84th percentile range of $\log(t_{\rm pk,rest})$ within each bin, while the vertical error bars indicate the bootstrap 68% confidence intervals on the mean $\log(L_{\rm avg,f,rest})$. The black dashed line represents the Bayesian regression fitted to the individual flare measurements, with $\beta=-1.60\pm 0.12$, while the blue solid line shows the separate fit to the binned geometric mean luminosities, yielding $\beta=-1.65^{+0.24}_{-0.20}$. The two slopes are consistent within their uncertainties.
figures.label: Fig. 5
figures.physical_core: Rest-frame average flare luminosity $L_{\rm avg,f,rest}=E_{\rm iso,f,rest}/w_{\rm rest}$ declines with peak time as $\beta\approx-1.6$ for the combined sample (individual fit $\beta=-1.60\pm0.12$; binned geometric means $\beta=-1.65^{+0.24}_{-0.20}$). The anti-correlation is significant for early–narrow flares but not for late–wide flares, giving only an indirect test of accretion-powered jet luminosity evolution.

figures.caption: Figure 4: Relation between the rest-frame flare peak time, $t_{\rm pk,rest}$, and the flare isotropic energy, $E_{\rm iso,f,rest}$ (left), and between the rest-frame flare width, $w_{\rm rest}$, and $E_{\rm iso,f,rest}$ (right). The purple and green points represent the early–narrow (Cluster 0; 78 flares) and late–wide (Cluster 1; 19 flares) flare populations, respectively. The error bars correspond to the $1\sigma$ uncertainties. The dashed lines show the median Bayesian linear regressions obtained using the method of Kelly [25], which accounts for measurement uncertainties in both variables as well as intrinsic scatter. For the $t_{\rm pk,rest}$ – $E_{\rm iso,f,rest}$ relation, we obtain $\beta=-0.14^{+0.05}_{-0.06}$ ($\alpha=9.3^{+2.8}_{-2.4}$) for the early–narrow flares and $\beta=0.05^{+0.07}_{-0.07}$ ($\alpha=1.1^{+3.5}_{-3.7}$) for the late–wide flares. Similarly, for the $w_{\rm rest}$ – $E_{\rm iso,f,rest}$ relation, we find $\beta=-0.03^{+0.08}_{-0.09}$ ($\alpha=3.6^{+4.4}_{-3.9}$) and $\beta=0.07^{+0.11}_{-0.10}$ ($\alpha=0.5^{+5.1}_{-5.3}$) for the early–narrow and late–wide flare populations, respectively. In both panels, the inferred slopes are consistent with zero within the $1\sigma$ credible intervals, indicating that the isotropic flare energy is not strongly coupled to either the flare peak time or flare width.
figures.label: Fig. 4
figures.physical_core: Bayesian regressions of $E_{\rm iso,f,rest}$ versus $t_{\rm pk,rest}$ and versus $w_{\rm rest}$ yield slopes consistent with zero for both clusters (early–narrow $\beta=-0.14^{+0.05}_{-0.06}$ and $-0.03^{+0.08}_{-0.09}$; late–wide $\beta=0.05^{+0.07}_{-0.07}$ and $0.07^{+0.11}_{-0.10}$), so isotropic flare energy is not strongly coupled to peak time or width.

analysis.reason: This off-nuclear TDE paper is relevant to photoionization and compact-object reprocessing, but it is not central to FRB, jet, neutrino, or supernova-engine work. Its useful increment is the optical C IV identification and the inferred compact reprocessing photosphere.
analysis.result: VLT spectra identify optical C IV $\lambda\lambda 5801,5812$ (C IV $\lambda 5805$) in off-nuclear TDE 2025abcr, at a projected offset of $9.3\,\mathrm{kpc}$ and $z\simeq 0.05$. The proposed excitation is continuum fluorescence plus photon trapping in the $312\,\mathrm{\AA}$ transition, analogous to WN winds and requiring strong EUV irradiation and high optical depth. A single-temperature fit gives $T_{\mathrm{BB}}\simeq 2\times 10^{4}\,\mathrm{K}$, below $3\times 10^{4}\,\mathrm{K}$ from the UV plus blue optical; the lack of rapid variability implies a reprocessing photosphere with $R\sim 10^{14}\,\mathrm{cm}$. Broad-line widths are relatively narrow, $\sim 2500$–$3000\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}}$, while He II and N III FWHM decline from $\sim 4000$–$5000\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}}$ to $\sim 2000\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}}$. Peak luminosity suggests $M_{\mathrm{BH}}\sim 10^{6}\,M_{\odot}$ with large uncertainty, and Swift/XRT detects $L_{X}\sim 10^{42}\,\mathrm{erg\,s^{-1}}$ ($0.3$–$10\,\mathrm{keV}$) without intrinsic absorption.
analysis.problem: The paper asks whether the feature near $5805\,\mathrm{\AA}$ in off-nuclear TDE 2025abcr is optical C IV $\lambda\lambda 5801,5812$, rather than shifted He I or [N II], and what its excitation implies for a compact, dense reprocessing region.
analysis.method: The analysis combines ZTF forced-PSF and LCOGT difference-imaging photometry, GTC/HiPERCAM and LCOGT intranight monitoring, and Swift/XRT–UVOT data with six VLT/FORS2 spectra ($R\simeq 900$) and one NOT/ALFOSC spectrum ($R\sim 300$), calibrated to contemporaneous photometry and corrected for $E(B-V)=0.013\,\mathrm{mag}$. A flat $\Lambda$CDM cosmology is adopted, the continuum is fit by a single-temperature blackbody, and each line by concentric double-Lorentzian components. Non-variability at the $0.008\,\mathrm{mag}$ ($g$) and $0.025\,\mathrm{mag}$ ($u$) levels is used to infer $R\sim 10^{14}\,\mathrm{cm}$.
assumptions: The absence of rapid variability is interpreted as emission from an extended, reprocessing-dominated optical photosphere.

analysis.research_progress: The advance is an off-nuclear TDE with Bowen fluorescence, a relatively small blackbody radius, and narrower broad lines, together with a reprocessing photosphere at $R\sim 10^{14}\,\mathrm{cm}$. Optical C IV, uncommon in AGN but known in supernova flash spectra and Wolf–Rayet stars, links the TDE envelope to a dense, strongly irradiated line-forming region, although quantitative gas constraints still require radiative-transfer modeling and ultraviolet spectra.

figures.caption: Figure 6: Schematic of the excitation and radiative decay pathways of C 3+. The gray arrow denotes photoionization to C 4+ in the recombination scenario, the blue arrow denotes continuum pumping near $312$ Å, and the green dashed arrows indicate radiative decay pathways. The numbered labels identify three stages relevant to fluorescence-powered optical C IV emission: (1) formation of C 3+ through photoionization; (2) excitation from the $2s$ ground state to the $3p$ levels by absorption of EUV continuum photons; and (3) trapping of photons in the $312$ Å transition, which enhances conversion into the C IV $\lambda\lambda 5801,5812$ doublet through the alternative $3p\rightarrow 3s$ decay channel. Subsequent decay through the $2p$ levels produces the ultraviolet C IV $\lambda\lambda 1548,1551$ doublet. Selected recombination-cascade pathways are also shown for comparison.
figures.label: Fig. 6
figures.physical_core: Excitation and decay pathways of C^{3+}: photoionization to C^{4+}, EUV continuum pumping near 312 Å from the 2s ground state to 3p, photon trapping that favors the 3p→3s channel producing optical C IV λλ5801,5812, and subsequent decay yielding UV C IV λλ1548,1551, contrasted with recombination cascades.

analysis.reason: This is a compact-object high-energy result: long-term Fermi-LAT and NuSTAR data show that Crab pulsed GeV and X-ray flux and photon index vary and are anti-correlated, testing the steady-pulsar assumption. It is incremental for magnetospheric emission and spin-down, but not central to FRB, supernova-engine, jet, or neutrino studies.
analysis.result: Pulsed Crab emission is not steady. The mean gamma-ray flux is $F_{\gamma}=(1.283\pm0.004)\times10^{-9}\,\mathrm{erg\,cm^{-2}\,s^{-1}}$ (0.1–100 GeV), with month-scale deviations from a few percent to $\sim20\%$, and $\Gamma_{\gamma}\approx2.17\pm0.02$ varying by up to $\sim10\%$. Linear slopes $(-2.65\pm0.94)\times10^{-12}\,\mathrm{erg\,cm^{-2}\,s^{-1}\,yr^{-1}}$ and $(-1.92\pm0.59)\times10^{-3}\,\mathrm{yr^{-1}}$ are poor descriptions ($\chi^2_{\nu}=1.9$, $p=2.6\times10^{-14}$; $\chi^2_{\nu}=2.7$, $p=6.8\times10^{-32}$). The X-ray means are $F_{\rm X}=(6.086\pm0.002)\times10^{-9}\,\mathrm{erg\,cm^{-2}\,s^{-1}}$ and $\Gamma_{\rm X}=1.80\pm0.05$, with slopes $(-7.95\pm0.69)\times10^{-11}\,\mathrm{erg\,cm^{-2}\,s^{-1}\,yr^{-1}}$ and $(+5.37\pm1.95)\times10^{-3}\,\mathrm{yr^{-1}}$. Flux and photon index are anti-correlated (brighter-when-harder), with $r_{\rm s}=-0.35$ ($p=4.0\times10^{-7}$) and $r_{\rm s}=-0.63$ ($p=5.5\times10^{-6}$). Nebular synchrotron, inverse-Compton, and total fluxes are not significantly correlated with the pulsed flux.
analysis.problem: The work tests whether Crab pulsed high-energy emission is steady on timescales much longer than the rotation period, except for a smooth secular decline from pulsar aging, and how braking-index deviations could arise if $I$, $\mu$, or $\alpha$ change.
analysis.method: Archival Fermi-LAT data (MJD 54710–60842, 100 MeV–100 GeV, about 17 yr, monthly integrals) and NuSTAR data (3.0–79.0 keV, about 13 yr) are phase-gated into pulsed and nebular spectra, with $1\sigma$ statistical plus systematic errors. Pulsed fits use $\mathrm{tbabs}\times\mathrm{powerlaw}$; nebular $N_{\rm H}=0.36\times10^{22}\,\mathrm{cm^{-2}}$ is fixed, $\Gamma_{\rm X}$ and normalization are tied within an epoch, and a 3% systematic uncertainty is included. Absorption uses the cited photoelectric cross sections. The braking index is $n=\Omega\ddot{\Omega}/\dot{\Omega}^{2}$, with spin parameters from the Jodrell Bank monthly ephemeris and $\ddot{\Omega}$ from adjacent $\dot{\Omega}$ differences. Magnetic-dipole spin-down power scales as $I\Omega\dot{\Omega}$.
assumptions: Pulsed Crab emission was taken to be steady on timescales much longer than the pulsation period, except for a smooth secular decrease associated with pulsar aging.
limits: The steadiness hypothesis under test applies only to timescales much larger than the pulsation period; the emission mechanism is not given a quantitative model.
citation_leads: Flux Variation of the Crab Pulsar Observed Using Fermi LAT and NuSTAR: “is considered to be steady over time scales much larger than the pulsation period”
Flux Variation of the Crab Pulsar Observed Using Fermi LAT and NuSTAR: “except for a smooth, secular decrease related to the aging of pulsars.”
Main: “discovery of variation in the flux and photon index of pulsed gamma-ray and X-ray emissions”
Main: “pulsed gamma-ray and X-ray emissions from the Crab pulsar and the anti-correlations between them.”
The braking index: “The braking index $n$ is defined by the rotational kinematics of the pulsar as $n=\Omega\ddot{\Omega}/\dot{\Omega}^{2}$.”
analysis.research_progress: The advance is a direct empirical detection that pulsed gamma-ray and X-ray flux and photon index both vary and are anti-correlated, rather than following only smooth aging. Matching magnetic-dipole braking would require at least one of $\dot{I}/I$, $\dot{\mu}/\mu$, and $\dot{\alpha}/\tan\alpha$ to vary coherently near $10^{-8}\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}$ while their random difference is thousands of times smaller; an added surface-temperature dependence could permit percent-level changes on monthly or shorter scales.

analysis.reason: Resolved SNR–molecular-cloud shocks and an elevated cosmic-ray ionization rate in W49B quantify supernova mechanical and cosmic-ray feedback, but the paper does not address central engines, shock breakout, jets, FRBs, or neutrinos.
analysis.result: Twelve western regions show HCO$^{+}$ and $^{12}$CO lines with FWHM $25$–$60\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}}$. Non-LTE analysis gives $n=(0.5$–$1.6)\times10^{5}\,\mathrm{cm^{-3}}$ and $N_{\rm HCO^{+}}/N_{\rm CO}=(4.2$–$14.5)\times10^{-4}$. Matching this ratio requires $\zeta_{\rm CR}$ of a few $\times10^{-14}$–$10^{-13}\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}$, compared with the standard $2.5\times10^{-17}\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}$. From $+75$ to $+100$ versus $+100$ to $+125\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}}$, the beam-averaged ratio rises from $(5.8\pm0.4)\times10^{-4}$ to $(8.5\pm0.8)\times10^{-4}$. With $t_{\rm loss}(E)\sim E/[L_{\rm p}(E)n_{\rm H_2}v(E)]$ and $n_{\rm H_2}=6.3\times10^{4}\,\mathrm{cm^{-3}}$, $10$ and $100\,\mathrm{MeV}$ protons cool in $\sim1.2$ and $\sim39\,\mathrm{yr}$; diffusion bounds are $D(10\,\mathrm{MeV})>2.8\times10^{24}$ and $D(100\,\mathrm{MeV})>8.0\times10^{22}\,\mathrm{cm^{2}\,s^{-1}}$. Clump kinetic energy exceeds cumulative cosmic-ray and X-ray heating, and cosmic-ray heating exceeds X-ray heating.

analysis.problem: The relative contributions of shocks, radiation, and cosmic rays to supernova feedback on molecular clouds are poorly constrained; in W49B the previously unresolved HCO$^{+}$/$^{12}$CO intensity ratio is $1$–$2$ orders of magnitude above typical molecular clouds.
analysis.method: ALMA 12 m/ACA and APEX map HCO$^{+}$ $J=1$–$0$, $3$–$2$, $4$–$3$ and $^{12}$CO $J=3$–$2$; imaging uses CASA tclean with hogbom, Briggs robust $=0.5$, and feathering, with line ratios at $8.5''$. RADEX non-LTE models and Paris–Durham steady planar shocks ($V_{\rm shock}=20$–$55\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}}$) are compared through MCMC, with proton losses $t_{\rm loss}(E)\sim E/[L_{\rm p}(E)n_{\rm H_2}v(E)]$.
assumptions: Where kinetic temperature does not converge, the non-LTE solutions fix $T_{\rm kin}$ at $100\,\mathrm{K}$ or $200\,\mathrm{K}$.

analysis.result: For 10 blazars (3 BL Lacs and 7 FSRQs) with >100 Steward SPOL measurements each during 2008–2018 at $\lambda=500$–$700\,\mathrm{nm}$, V-band flux and $\mathrm{PD}=\sqrt{q^{2}+u^{2}}$ are generally better described by a log-normal distribution than by a Gaussian or Rice distribution. Exceptions are the flux of 3C 273 (Gaussian) and the PD of PKS 2155$-$304 (Rice). ZDCF flux–PD correlation peaks are about $0.53$–$0.93$; PD has high relative variability amplitude $\mathrm{RVA}=(F_{\rm max}-F_{\rm min})/F_{\rm max}$ and an approximately linear rms–PD trend. Successive perturbations $\vec{B}_{n+1}=\vec{B}_{n}(1+\delta_n)$ accumulate as $\vec{B}=\vec{B}_{0}\prod_{i=1}^{N}(1+\delta_i)$.
analysis.problem: The physical origin of large optical polarization-degree changes in blazar jets is unclear: long-term flux variability is often ascribed to multiplicative processes because it is log-normal, but it is not established whether PD variability has the same origin rather than arising from linearly superposed independent zones.
analysis.method: Daily Bayesian blocks ($p_0=0.01$) are applied to V-band flux and PD. Variability is quantified by $F_{\rm var}=\sqrt{(S^{2}-E^{2})/F^{2}}$, $F=\sigma_{\rm LC}^{2}/\sigma^{2}$ with critical value 6.636, RVA, and ANOVA. Gaussian, log-normal, and Rice models are compared using $\mathrm{AIC}=2k-2\ln(L)$, $\mathrm{BIC}=k\ln(n)-2\ln(L)$, Anderson–Darling tests, and $\chi_r^{2}$; the log-normal PDF is $f(x)=1/(x\sigma\sqrt{2\pi})\exp[-(\ln x-\mu)^{2}/(2\sigma^{2})]$. Interpretation uses transverse-shock, helical-field, and TEMZ models and $\partial\vec{B}/\partial t=\vec{\nabla}\times(\vec{v}\times\vec{B})+\eta\vec{\nabla}^{2}\vec{B}$.

analysis.reason: The paper is useful for supernova-remnant shock–cloud interactions and multi-messenger tests because it ties two-component gamma-ray spectra to reaccelerated background protons and predicts pp neutrinos, but it is not centered on FRBs, central engines, or relativistic jets.
analysis.result: The baseline photon spectrum is $\frac{d\Phi_{\gamma}}{dE_{\gamma}}=\frac{d\Phi_{\pi^{0},\mathrm{re}}}{dE_{\gamma}}+\frac{d\Phi_{\mathrm{IC},\mathrm{fresh}}}{dE_{\gamma}}$. In low-density regions surrounded by dense molecular clumps the two components form clearly separated peaks; in a dense environment with an additional nearby clump they overlap more smoothly and the high-energy part is mainly a broad shoulder. The low-energy bump is primarily $\pi^{0}$ emission from background cosmic rays compressed and reaccelerated in dense clouds, while the harder high-energy component is usually inverse Compton from freshly accelerated electrons and can instead be hadronic when the gas density is high. The neutrino flux is predicted from the gamma-ray-constrained proton spectrum and is not a fixed fraction of the total gamma-ray flux. Reported source scales include CTB 80 at $d=2\,\mathrm{kpc}$, W44 at about $20\,\mathrm{kyr}$ and $2.2\,\mathrm{kpc}$, $\gamma$ Cygni at about $7\,\mathrm{kyr}$, $1.7\,\mathrm{kpc}$ and radius about $15\,\mathrm{pc}$, W51C at about $5.5\,\mathrm{kpc}$ with atomic-hydrogen density about $30$–$160\,\mathrm{cm^{-3}}$, and 1LHAASO J1852+0050u above $100\,\mathrm{TeV}$ with molecular-cloud density about $360\,\mathrm{cm^{-3}}$. Near HESS J1731-347 the diffusion coefficient can be about $3$–$20$ times below the usual Galactic-disk value.
analysis.problem: The paper asks whether the two-component gamma-ray spectra of these cosmic-ray sources have a common physical origin and how the surrounding density structure changes the separation of the components.
analysis.method: GALPROP supplies the spatially dependent background cosmic rays, with $D_{xx}(r,z,\mathcal{R})=D_{0}F(r,z)\,\beta^{\eta}(\mathcal{R}/\mathcal{R}_{0})^{\delta_{0}F(r,z)}$, $D_{0}=4.8\times10^{28}\,\mathrm{cm^{2}\,s^{-1}}$ and $\delta_{0}=0.63$. Shock reacceleration may be steepened by ion–neutral damping through $f_{\mathrm{sh}}(p)=f_{\mathrm{acc}}(p)\,\mathcal{B}(p)$, where $\mathcal{B}=1$ below $p_{\mathrm{br}}$ and $\mathcal{B}=p_{\mathrm{br}}/p$ above it. Compression $s\equiv n_m/n_d=n_m/(r_{\mathrm{sh}}n_0)$ maps momenta as $p\to s^{1/3}p$ and gives $n_{p,\mathrm{ad}}(p)=s^{2/3}n_{p,\mathrm{sh}}(s^{-1/3}p)$; accumulation then follows $\partial N_p/\partial t=\partial_p[b_p N_p]+Q_p$. Fresh particles supply the second component, and neutrinos are calculated from the same $p$–$p$ proton and gas model without a separate normalization.
assumptions: A low shock velocity alone is not assumed to preserve the original background spectral shape after reacceleration.
limits: The neutrino spectrum is a theoretical prediction of the gamma-ray-constrained proton model, not a fit to neutrino observations or a fixed rescaling of the total gamma-ray flux.
citation_leads: Two-component $gamma$-Ray Structure from the CR Sources: “Sources located in low-density environments but surrounded by dense molecular clumps exhibit two clearly separated”
2.3 Shock Reacceleration and Adiabatic Compression of Background Protons: “A low shock velocity alone therefore does not justify assuming that the reaccelerated spectrum”
3 Results and Discussion: “not obtained by converting the observed total gamma-ray flux using a fixed proportionality factor.”
4 Conclusion and Summary: “The low-energy bump originates primarily from background cosmic rays in dense molecular clouds.”
analysis.research_progress: The work extends the earlier two-component cosmic-ray emission picture to additional observed sources and links spectral morphology to environment: separated peaks occur around low-density sources enclosed by dense clumps, whereas dense-source geometries produce smoother overlap. Its multi-messenger increment is the source-by-source $p$–$p$ neutrino prediction, rather than a universal gamma-to-neutrino conversion factor, testing local high-energy cosmic rays against a collective low-energy Galactic background.

analysis.reason: This NuSTAR study of the NGC 4151 corona is adjacent to the group's neutrino and compact high-energy interests: it quantifies thermal Compton balance and tests whether neutrinos or X17 pairs can compete with Compton cooling, but it is not an FRB, supernova-engine, or jet-breakout paper.
analysis.result: The hard X-ray continuum is thermal Comptonization with $kT_{\rm e}\approx 40-125$ keV and slab $\tau\approx 0.4-1.2$. $kT_{\rm e}$ and $\tau$ are anticorrelated at Compton parameter $\gamma\approx 3.12$ (historical $y\approx 1$; bright states $kT_{\rm e}\approx 40-100$ keV, $\tau\approx 1-2$). Variability gives $\tau_{\rm var}\approx 5-28$ h, $R\approx 250-1200\,r_g$ and $\ell\approx 0.5-3.7$, below pair runaway. $L_\nu/L_X\approx 3\times 10^{-3}$ does not displace Compton cooling. For $\sim 8.5$ MeV X17 $e^\pm$ injection, $t_{\rm th}\sim 0.82-24$ h exceeds Compton cooling ($0.07-0.45$ h); extra pairs do not change $kT_{\rm e}$ or $\tau$ unless injection greatly exceeds photoproduction.
analysis.problem: What sets the thermal balance of the NGC 4151 hot corona, and can neutrino losses or X17-induced pairs alter the observed $kT_{\rm e}$–$\tau$ thermostat?
analysis.method: Fourteen NuSTAR spectra were reduced in HEASoft (60 arcsec source region, background subtraction, 3600 s light curves) and fit with tbabs+zpcfabs+nthcomp+pexrav+zgauss. Slab $\tau$ is derived from $\Gamma$ and $kT_{\rm e}$ with the Sunyaev & Titarchuk (1980) relation, avoiding the spherical Eq. (14) factor of 3. Flux changes $>3\sigma$ define $\tau_{\rm var}$, then $R<c\tau_{\rm var}/(1+z)$ and $\ell=\sigma_T L_X/(R m_e c^3)$. X17 effects are judged by comparing Coulomb $t_{\rm th}$ and photoproduced $n_\pm$ from slab $u_{\rm rad}$ with the Compton cooling time.
assumptions: A slab corona is used rather than the spherical Sunyaev & Titarchuk Eq. (14), as suggested by polarization observations.
limits: The X17 decay time is of order a picosecond, so a direct-detection instrument is not considered.

analysis.reason: This is a standard XPoSat/XSPECT spectral–timing study of thermal accretion-state evolution in the persistent black-hole HMXB LMC X–3. It has no substantial link to FRB/PRS, supernova central engines, shock breakout, CSM interaction, relativistic jets, neutrinos, or dispersion-measure physics.
analysis.result: Between the 2024 and 2025 XSPECT campaigns the source moved from a harder, fainter, more variable interval to a brighter, softer, less variable state. Epoch-averaged fits of $\mathrm{tbabs}\times\mathrm{diskbb}$ give $kT_{\rm in}=0.837\pm0.005\,\mathrm{keV}$ (2024, soft segment only; $N_{\rm H}$ frozen at $0.01\times10^{22}\,\mathrm{cm}^{-2}$) and $kT_{\rm in}=1.167\pm0.004\,\mathrm{keV}$ (2025), with unabsorbed flux rising from $(1.964\pm0.002)$ to $(9.585\pm0.004)\times10^{-10}\,\mathrm{erg}\,\mathrm{cm}^{-2}\,\mathrm{s}^{-1}$ (about fivefold). Disk normalizations are $24.8\pm0.7$ and $29.1\pm0.5$. The 2024 PDS has excess power below $\sim0.05\,\mathrm{Hz}$; neither epoch shows a significant QPO or soft–hard lag. For $D\sim50\,\mathrm{kpc}$ and $i\sim67^{\circ}$, the 2025 normalization implies an apparent inner radius $\sim43\,\mathrm{km}$ and a corrected radius $\sim50\,\mathrm{km}$, close to an ISCO of $\sim53\,\mathrm{km}$ for $M\sim7\,M_{\odot}$ and $a_{\ast}\approx0.25$.
analysis.problem: How the luminosity, spectral hardness, and rapid variability of persistent LMC X–3 change between the 2024 and 2025 XSPECT epochs, and whether that change is the usual shift toward a stable, thermally dominated disk.
analysis.method: Public Level-2 XSPECT data (0.8–15 keV; analysis uses $2^{\circ}\times2^{\circ}$ detectors) were flare-filtered, merged by epoch, and reduced with the standard pipeline. Hardness is the 2.0–10.0 keV to 0.8–2.0 keV count-rate ratio on 500 s bins; HIDs and hardness–rms diagrams use sigma-clipped light curves. PDS use the Belloni fractional-rms normalization, and soft–hard delays use 10 ms cross-correlation. Spectra are fit in XSPEC 12.14 with $\chi^{2}$ and 68% errors; the adopted model is $\mathrm{tbabs}\times\mathrm{diskbb}$, while $\mathrm{tbabs}\times\mathrm{powerlaw}$ and $\mathrm{tbabs}\times(\mathrm{diskbb}+\mathrm{powerlaw})$ fit worse. The disk normalization is $\mathrm{Norm}_{\rm disk}=\left(\frac{R_{\rm in}/\mathrm{km}}{D/10\,\mathrm{kpc}}\right)^{2}\cos i$.
assumptions: A distance of $\sim50\,\mathrm{kpc}$ and inclination $\sim67^{\circ}$ are assumed when converting the 2025 diskbb normalization to an apparent inner radius.
limits: The diskbb normalization alone cannot provide a precise inner-disk radius because of uncertainties in the colour-correction factor, inclination, and relativistic effects, and this work does not independently locate the ISCO.

analysis.result: Along fixed-$\hat{s}$ adiabats the allowed region shrinks monotonically as temperature rises. The DD2/DD-MEX exit boundary runs from $(\mu_{\mathrm{B}},T)\simeq(2.16\,\mathrm{GeV},0)$ to $(1.55\,\mathrm{GeV},152\,\mathrm{MeV})$, crossing $n_{\mathrm{B}}^{c}=0.85\,\mathrm{fm^{-3}}$ at $T\simeq 125\,\mathrm{MeV}$.

analysis.problem: The model-independent pQCD equation-of-state bound had been established only for cold, catalyzed matter, leaving open whether it constrains the hot, dense matter in binary neutron-star mergers, core-collapse supernovae, and proto-neutron stars.
analysis.method: The Komoltsev–Kurkela construction is applied on adiabats of fixed $\hat{s}\equiv s/n_{\mathrm{B}}$ after replacing $\mu_{\mathrm{B}}$ by the specific enthalpy $h=(\varepsilon+p)/n_{\mathrm{B}}=\mu_{\mathrm{B}}+T\hat{s}$, using $\mathrm{d}p=n_{\mathrm{B}}\,\mathrm{d}h$ and $c_{s}^{2}=(\mathrm{d}\ln h/\mathrm{d}\ln n_{\mathrm{B}})_{\hat{s}}$. The low anchor is HS(DD2) at $n_{\mathrm{B}}=0.176\,\mathrm{fm^{-3}}$ and the high anchor is scale-averaged pQCD at $n_{\mathrm{B}}=6.5\,\mathrm{fm^{-3}}$, with $\bar{\Lambda}=\sqrt{(0.722\times 4\pi T X_{\mathrm{lat}})^{2}+(2\mu_{\mathrm{B}}X/3)^{2}}$ log-uniformly averaged over $X\in[0.5,2.0]$. Closed-form $(h,n_{\mathrm{B}})$ and $(\varepsilon,p)$ boundaries are tested on 11 RMF models and 500 samples from each of the DDH and NL posteriors.
assumptions: Matter is neutrino-transparent, charge-neutral, and in beta equilibrium, so $h=\mu_{\mathrm{B}}+T\hat{s}$.
limits: The bound acts at densities that isentropic DD2 stars do not reach; whether merger remnants approach it must be judged with simulation data.

analysis.research_progress: The $T=0$ bound carries over exactly under $\mu_{\mathrm{B}}\to h$ because $\mathrm{d}p=n_{\mathrm{B}}\,\mathrm{d}h$ at fixed $\hat{s}$. The thermal weakening of nuclear models follows $n^{*}(\hat{s})=A/(1+B\hat{s}^{C})$, with $(A,B,C)=(1.01,0.016,1.97)$ for DD2 and $(0.91,0.016,1.85)$ for DD-MEX; nearly universal $B$ and $C$ indicate that the shape is set by pQCD/causality geometry while $A$ carries the low-density nuclear physics. Cold pQCD consistency therefore does not guarantee consistency on finite-entropy adiabats.

analysis.result: Among O5-detectable lensed mergers, about 60% of BNS kilonovae and 10% of NSBH kilonovae are observable in one LSST exposure, mostly as quads. Resolved BNS fractions are $51\%$ ($g$), $40\%$ ($r$), and $30\%$ ($i$), rising to $58\%$ in $g$ for unresolved images. NSBH-gen yields at most $\sim 2.3\%$ above a single-exposure limit. The fit index is $\mathrm{DI_{BNS}}=c_1\log(\mu)+c_2\log(M)+c_3\log(q)+c_4\log(|\cos\iota|)+c_5\log(D_L)$, plus $d_6\log(\chi)$ for NSBH.

analysis.method: Lensed sources are sampled from the lensing-weighted Madau–Dickinson distribution $p(z_s,\mathcal{H}_L)=p(z_s)P(\mathcal{H}_L|z_s)$, with $\tau(z_s)=4.17\times10^{-6}(D^{c}(z_s)/\mathrm{Gpc})^{3}$. MOSFiT BNS-gen/NSBH-gen and POSSIS light curves are scaled by magnification and delay; joint detection requires two images with $\mathrm{SNR}>8$ and a peak brighter than the LSST limit, summarized by logistic $\mathrm{DI}$.

source_sections: New Constraints on the Ultrahigh Energy Neutrino Flux from the First Array-Wide Search with the Askaryan Radio Array

analysis.reason: This first array-wide ARA diffuse search is directly relevant to ultrahigh-energy neutrino and UHECR-source studies: zero events set the leading flux limit at $50$–$1000\,\mathrm{EeV}$ and exclude some trans-GZK proton source models.
analysis.result: The array-wide diffuse search observes $n=0$ events against an expected background of $0.13\pm 0.01$ (stat.) $^{+0.05}_{-0.06}$ (syst.). The Feldman–Cousins $90\%$ CL limit is the strongest among techniques over $50$–$1000\,\mathrm{EeV}$. Analysis-level expectations are $\mu=5.3$ (Global UL; $2.6\sigma$, $99\%$ exclusion), $\mu=2.4$ (Muzio; $1.3\sigma$, $90\%$ exclusion), $\mu=1.6$ (KM3NeT; $0.8\sigma$, $77\%$), $\mu=0.4$ (Kotera; $27\%$), and $\mu=0.2$ for both $100\%$ protons and Fang pulsars ($<1\%$). Low-energy systematics are $\sim 50\%$ (Askaryan model) and high-energy systematics $\sim 150\%$ (neutrino–nucleon cross section).
analysis.method: ARA stations A1–A5 plus the A5 phased array are analyzed from January 2013 through December 2023, corresponding to $28$ station-years ($25.9$ after quality cuts; $10.6$ array-equivalent years). Each string uses $150$–$850\,\mathrm{MHz}$ antennas with station triggers kept at $\le 5$ events/s and the phased array at $\le 11$ events/s. Sensitivity for $50$ configurations is computed with NuLeptonSim and AraSim for an $E^{-1}$ spectrum. Cuts were set on a random $10\%$ sample with the remaining $90\%$ blinded; surface and thermal cuts retain $56\%$ and $85\%$ of simulated $E^{-1}$ neutrinos, and the benchmark-flux efficiency is $28\%$. Models are tested with $p=\mathrm{Poiss}(n=0\mid\mu)$ and Feldman–Cousins $90\%$ CL limits.
limits: The search observes $0$ events on a background of $0.13\pm 0.01$ (stat.) $^{+0.05}_{-0.06}$ (syst.), so the outcome is an upper limit rather than a detection.

analysis.research_progress: This is the first full-array, full-livetime ARA diffuse $\mathrm{UHE}\nu$ search. With $n=0$ and background $0.13\pm 0.01$, it provides the strongest $50$–$1000\,\mathrm{EeV}$ limit in a band complementary to optical Cherenkov and particle detectors, excludes the Muzio trans-GZK proton model at $90\%$ CL ($\mu=2.4$), and leaves Kotera, pure-proton, and Fang-pulsar scenarios with $\mu=0.2$–$0.4$ essentially unconstrained under $p=\mathrm{Poiss}(n=0\mid\mu)$.

The tail of the surface background population is parametrized as a KDE in elevation, while the tail of the thermal background population is parametrized as an exponential in LDA score. The long tails of these populations force the optimizer to set strong cuts even while the bulk is compact. We note that the distribution of thermal events in elevation is biased due to known instrumental artifacts that arise when correlating low SNR events [ 22, 33 ].

analysis.reason: This five-station ARA diffuse-flux search is relevant because its null result and 90% CL limits test cosmogenic and compact-object (trans-GZK and pulsar) neutrino scenarios, but it is mainly an analysis-methodology update rather than a source-physics result on FRBs, supernova engines, or jets.
analysis.result: With an effective livetime of $10.6$ yr ($25.9$ station-years after quality cuts), no neutrino candidate remains. The single phased-array event ($\mathrm{SNR}\sim 12$, elevation $-35^\circ$) is local A5 detector emission. The expected background is $0.13\pm 0.01\,(\mathrm{stat.})^{+0.05}_{-0.06}\,(\mathrm{syst.})$, from $b_{\mathrm{surf}}=4.50^{+1.01}_{-0.85}\times 10^{-2}$ and $b_{\mathrm{therm}}=8.65^{+0.44}_{-0.28}\times 10^{-2}$, giving a $5\sigma$ threshold $n_{\mathrm{disc}}=4$. Analysis efficiency is $28\%$ for a flux at current experimental upper limits. The $90\%$ CL all-flavor limit is the strongest reported at $50$–$1000\,\mathrm{EeV}$ and excludes the Muzio trans-GZK model. Analysis-level expectations are Global UL $5.3$ ($\epsilon=27.6\%$), Muzio $2.4$ ($21.8\%$), Kotera $0.4$ ($21.1\%$), $100\%$ protons $0.2$ ($25.0\%$), Fang pulsars $0.2$ ($16.7\%$), and KM3NeT $1.6$ ($13.8\%$).
analysis.problem:
Whether a diffuse flux of ultrahigh-energy neutrinos, $E_
u\gtrsim 100\,\mathrm{PeV}$, including cosmogenic neutrinos from UHECR interactions with the CMB and EBL, is detectable through in-ice Askaryan radio pulses. UHECRs ($E_{\mathrm{CR}}\gtrsim 1\,\mathrm{EeV}$) are mostly extragalactic heavy nuclei whose magnetic deflections block source tracing, while protons are GZK-suppressed above $\sim 10^{19.7}\,\mathrm{eV}$; near $1\,\mathrm{EeV}$, IceCube and ANITA give $E_
u^2\Phi_
u\lesssim 10^{-8}\,\mathrm{GeV}\,\mathrm{cm}^{-2}\,\mathrm{s}^{-1}\,\mathrm{sr}^{-1}$.
analysis.method: Five ARA stations (2013–2023) are analyzed with $10\%$ of data for background design and $90\%$ blinded. NuLeptonSim generates $E^{-1}$ neutrinos from $10^{16}$–$10^{21}\,\mathrm{eV}$ for later reweighting inside a fiducial cylinder, using Connolly cross sections and PREM; AraSim models the stations. AraProc22 calibrates waveforms and applies a $50$–$875\,\mathrm{MHz}$ bandpass. Signal strength is $\mathrm{SNR}=(V_{\mathrm{pp}}/2)/\mathrm{RMS}$. Direction uses $C_{ij}(\tau)$ with $n(z)=n_{\mathrm{ice}}-(n_{\mathrm{ice}}-n_{\mathrm{firn}})e^{-z/\Lambda}$ ($n_{\mathrm{ice}}=1.780$, $n_{\mathrm{firn}}=1.326$, $\Lambda\simeq 49.505\,\mathrm{m}$). Phased-array beams scale as signal $\propto N$ and noise $\propto\sqrt{N}$. Cuts minimize the $5\sigma$ discovery normalization at $E_0=10^{18.5}\,\mathrm{eV}$, $$\phi_0^{\mathrm{disc}}(\boldsymbol{\Sigma},\boldsymbol{\Theta})=\frac{\mathrm{FC}(n_{\mathrm{disc}}(B),B)}{\int f(E)\,\mathcal{E}(E)\,dE}.$$ Thermal separation uses impulsivity $\mathcal{I}=2\langle H\rangle-1$.
assumptions: A diffuse-flux neutrino is expected to produce an impulsive, nanosecond-scale Askaryan signal that originates in the ice and is seen in multiple antennas.
limits: The analysis efficiency is only $28\%$ for a neutrino flux at the current experimental upper limits.

Optimized background leakages are $b_{\mathrm{surf}}=4.50^{+1.01}_{-0.85}\times 10^{-2}$ and $b_{\mathrm{therm}}=8.65^{+0.44}_{-0.28}\times 10^{-2}$, totaling $B=0.13\pm 0.01$ before the separate systematic.

analysis.research_progress: This is the first ARA diffuse search using all five stations and $10.6$ yr, about three times the previous ARA exposure. analysis.result: No line-seed inverse-Compton candidate is shown to satisfy photon supply, relative components, LAT consistency, and escape together. In the observer-directed Thomson limit, $\epsilon^{\rm IC}_{\rm obs}\simeq 2\gamma_e^2\epsilon(1-\beta_e\mu_i)/(1+z)$, while a head-on collision approaches $4\gamma_e^2\epsilon/(1+z)$. For host-frame $Ly\alpha\simeq 10.2\,{\rm eV}$ and $H\alpha\simeq 1.89\,{\rm eV}$, scattering to $10\,{\rm MeV}$ needs $\gamma_{e,Ly\alpha}\simeq 531$ and $\gamma_{e,H\alpha}\simeq 1.23\times 10^3$. A log-normal electron distribution seeded by H$_2$ $2.122\,\mu{\rm m}$ ($0.584\,{\rm eV}$) matches two published intervals at $E_{\rm c,H_2}=11.5$ and $8.8\,{\rm MeV}$, with $\gamma_0=3.30\times 10^3$ and $2.69\times 10^3$ and $s_\gamma=0.087$ and $0.177$; the corresponding trial UV centroids are about $210$ and $161\,{\rm MeV}$ with standard deviations about $35$ and $55\,{\rm MeV}$. None of 40 molecular combinations lies below the adopted central envelope at all sampled energies, and trace minima are about $3.46$, $1.48$, $1.60$, and $1.40$. Even under ideal excitation and internal escape, compact reference-line densities fall short by factors of approximately $4$–$9$; precursor-assisted deficits remain at least about $4.3$, or about $87$–$1.7\times 10^2$ for single photon use. analysis.problem: Can H$_2$ ultraviolet-fluorescence photons, hydrogen recombination lines, or metal K-shell lines, scattered once by relativistic electrons, explain the Fermi-GBM MeV feature of GRB 221009A without violating the simultaneous LAT spectrum, local photon supply, timing, angular geometry, and the adopted spectral envelope?
analysis.method: The model uses anisotropic single-scattering kinematics and a Klein–Nishina emissivity. With recoil parameter $b\equiv 4\gamma_e\epsilon/(m_ec^2)$, the local response is $d\ln\epsilon^{\rm IC}_{\rm obs}/d\ln\epsilon=1/(1+b)$. The flux is $F_{\epsilon_{\rm obs}}(\epsilon_{\rm obs},t_{\rm obs})=\frac{1+z}{d_L^2}\int d^3\boldsymbol{r}\,j_{\rm IC}[(1+z)\epsilon_{\rm obs},\Omega_{\rm s},\boldsymbol{r},t_{\rm ret}]e^{-\tau_{\rm esc}}$, integrated on equal-arrival-time surfaces with $dt_{\rm obs}=(1+z)(1-\beta_e\mu_{\rm s})dt$. Electrons follow $\frac{dN_e}{d\ln\gamma_e}=\frac{N_e}{\sqrt{2\pi}s_\gamma}\exp\left[-\frac{(\ln\gamma_e-\ln\gamma_0)^2}{2s_\gamma^2}\right]$; $\gamma_0$ and $s_\gamma$ are calibrated to photon moments, and 40 PDR-template plus external-screen combinations are compared with reconstructed central spectra. Optically thin component ratios scale as $\frac{F_{2,B_2}}{F_{1,B_1}}=\frac{u_2}{u_1}\frac{\mathcal{P}_{2,B_2}}{\mathcal{P}_{1,B_1}}$.
assumptions: Ideal excitation and internal escape are assumed when estimating the compact reference-line photon density.

limits: None of the 40 molecular combinations satisfies the baseline central spectral envelope at all sampled energies, and the comparison is not a statistical exclusion.

analysis.result: A CNN with $\mathcal{N}=10^{3}$ templates reaches a sensitivity distance comparable to SFT matched filtering, which instead needs approximately $\mathcal{N}_{\mathrm{SFT}}=10^{7}$ templates, about four orders of magnitude more. For $f_{\max}=10\,\mathrm{Hz}$ and $f_{\min}\in\{2,3,4,5\}\,\mathrm{Hz}$, the quoted evaluation time falls from minutes to milliseconds, a speed-up of about $1.6\times10^{4}$–$4.0\times10^{4}$; the CNN per-template cost is $\langle\mathfrak{c}_1\rangle\approx(3$–$25)\,\mu\mathrm{s}$. At fixed template number, sensitivity follows $\langle s\rangle\sim\rho_{\rm opt}^{2}(1-\langle\mu\rangle)$ with $\rho_{\rm opt}^{2}\propto\int_{f_{\min}}^{10\,\mathrm{Hz}}f^{-7/3}/S_n(f)\,df$.
analysis.problem: Early warning of binary neutron-star inspirals in third-generation detectors is limited by the computing cost of evaluating the detection statistic at low latency.
analysis.method: Early inspirals are represented by narrowband SFTs with $T_{\mathrm{SFT}}=31\,\mathrm{s}$ and $\Delta k=51$ bins about $f(t;\mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{c}})=f_{\max}[1+(256/5)(\pi f_{\max})^{8/3}(G\mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{c}}/c^{3})^{5/3}(t_{\max}-t)]^{-3/8}$. A CNN minimizes binary cross-entropy and searches only $\mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{c}}$, while the SFT statistic $\mathcal{X}$ is maximized analytically over phase and luminosity distance and then over an eight-dimensional bank. Latency is modeled as $\mathcal{C}=\mathcal{N}\langle\mathfrak{c}_1\rangle$, with $f_s=40\,\mathrm{Hz}$ for the 3, 4, and 5 Hz regimes.
limits: For lower chirp masses, evolution from $f_{\min}$ to $f_{\max}$ can exceed the fixed analysis window, so the signal is aligned at $f_{\max}$ and only its late portion is retained.

analysis.reason: This ZTF spectroscopic census of hydrogen-rich SLSNe directly constrains circumstellar interaction, pre-explosion mass loss, and possible Ia-CSM contamination, which are central to supernova-engine and CSM studies.
analysis.result: Of 106 hydrogen-rich SLSNe, 105 show narrow Balmer emission and are spectroscopically SLSNe-IIn; SN 2022lvm is the sole broad-lined SLSN-II in the discussed 2021–2022 subset comparison (1/36, 2.8%). Measured $L_{\mathrm{H}\alpha}$ spans $2.2\times10^{40}$ to $1.5\times10^{42}\,\mathrm{erg\,s^{-1}}$ (median $2.6\times10^{41}\,\mathrm{erg\,s^{-1}}$). The median Balmer decrement rises from 2.85 before $+100$ d to 4.40 afterward, below the Ia-CSM comparison medians 6.58 and 17.76. After excluding the SLSN-II and six Ia-CSM-like objects, median shell speed correlates with peak magnitude ($r=0.63$, $p=0.010$): brighter events tend to have lower $v_{\rm s}$. For 13 calibrated objects at $v_{\rm CSM}=100\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}}$ and $\epsilon=0.5$, $\dot{M}\sim0.028$–$0.30\,M_{\odot}\,\mathrm{yr^{-1}}$ from $L=\frac{1}{2}\epsilon\dot{M}v_{\rm s}^{3}/u_{\rm w}$. Six of 105 narrow-line events ($\sim6\%$) are Ia-CSM-like. Narrow interaction lines can persist beyond $+200$ d, with no Balmer morphology unique to SLSNe-IIn relative to fainter SNe IIn.
analysis.problem: Whether luminous narrow-line SLSNe-IIn are spectroscopically only the bright extreme of SNe IIn, what dense hydrogen-rich CSM and enhanced pre-explosion mass loss they require, and whether narrow Balmer lines plus high luminosity uniquely imply core collapse rather than Ia-CSM.
analysis.method: The study uses 304 optical spectra of 106 ZTF events selected at rest-frame peak $M\leq-19.9$ mag, with phases $(t-t_{\rm peak})/(1+z)$ and fluxes scaled by $10^{-0.4(m_{\rm GP}-m_{\rm syn})}$ from Gaussian-process light curves (287 absolutely calibrated). Balmer luminosity, pEW and FWHM are measured after local continuum subtraction. Single-epoch Monte Carlo electron-scattering snapshots (escatter; $10^{5}$ H$\alpha$ photons outside a cold dense shell) fit line profiles. Mass-loss rates use $L=\frac{1}{2}\epsilon\dot{M}\frac{v_{\rm s}^{3}}{u_{\rm w}}$ and $\dot{M}=\frac{2L}{\epsilon}\frac{u_{\rm w}}{v_{\rm s}^{3}}$, with luminosity integrated from the spectra and a blackbody extension to 3000–20000 Å.
assumptions: Quoted mass-loss rates use the adopted CSM-interaction model with $\epsilon=0.5$ and $v_{\rm CSM}=100\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}}$, commonly with a shock speed of $5000\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}}$.
limits: Inferred mass-loss rates are order-of-magnitude estimates rather than precise progenitor mass-loss histories.

analysis.result: Stochastic acceleration appreciably changes the downstream particle spectrum whenever $\eta \gtrsim \xi_{\rm CR}$. For standard Model I parameters, including stochastic acceleration and wave feedback increases the gamma-ray flux between $\sim 1$ and $100\,\mathrm{GeV}$ by $\sim 50\%$. For an undamped $f(p)\propto p^{-4}$ Kolmogorov cascade, $P t_{\rm age}/P_{\rm CR}\approx (3/4)\eta/\xi_{\rm CR}$; acceleration times scale as $\tau_{\rm acc}\sim p^{1/3}$ (Kolmogorov) or $\sim p^{1/2}$ (Kraichnan), while source-free inertial spectra are $W\sim k^{-5/3}$ and $W\sim k^{-3/2}$. analysis.result: Homogeneous collective precession (HCP) is a rotating-frame fixed point, but it is not always attracting. As the electron collision rate $\kappa_e$ approaches $0.0025$ from below, the target growth rate and the HCP number offset vanish together (supercritical Hopf); near $\kappa_e\simeq0.018$ a finite-amplitude pair appears, and the unstable branch merges with the target near $\kappa_e\simeq0.0221$ (subcritical Hopf). An independent HCP crossing occurs at $\kappa_e\simeq0.0200194578$, before target destabilization at $\kappa_e\simeq0.0221481171$. For $0.034\le\kappa_e\le0.060$, successive maxima of $P_z$ period-double eight times toward a stable $256$-cycle, with spacing ratios approaching $\delta_{\rm F}\simeq4.669$. At $\kappa_e=0.055025$ the leading Lyapunov estimate is $\widehat\lambda_1\simeq2.8\times10^{-3}$ for bounded irregular evolution. The HCP balance is $s(u^\star)^2=z^\star\tau^\star$, while averages obey $s[\langle u\rangle_T^2+\mathrm{Var}_T(u)]=\langle z\rangle_T\langle Z\rangle_T+\mathrm{Cov}_T(z,Z)-\tfrac12\mathcal{B}_{u^2}$. The largest reported HCP-versus-time-average population deviation is $8.03\%$, set by the mean coherent torque rather than by stationarity.
analysis.problem: The issue is whether a collisionally balanced HCP state attracts neutrino flavor trajectories or whether collisional flavor instability instead produces Hopf cycles, period doubling, and chaos, and how far HCP or mean-only estimates miss the time-averaged flavor populations.
analysis.method: The full quantum kinetic equations are linearized in the rotating frame, including the response of the self-interaction field; after removal of the common phase, local attraction requires all seven Jacobian eigenvalues to have negative real parts. For energy-independent rates the collective matrix follows the monochromatic kinetics and residuals contract at least as $e^{-\kappa_* t}$. Root number is fixed by the sign of $\mathcal{C}$, and $\kappa_e$ is scanned with multiple shooting and Lyapunov estimates. Steady balance is $s(u^\star)^2=z^\star\tau^\star$, whereas the time-averaged identity keeps $\mathrm{Var}_T(u)$ and $\mathrm{Cov}_T(z,Z)$.
assumptions: Existence of an HCP state does not imply attraction; attraction is judged by linearizing the full quantum kinetic equations in the rotating frame, including self-interaction response.
limits: Because of fluctuation and coherent-torque terms, an HCP estimate need not equal the time average; the maximum reported deviation is $8.03\%$, and relative spectral errors also depend on $c_E$.

analysis.reason: This is a low-latency BNS early-warning search method for third-generation detectors, useful for compact-object multi-messenger follow-up, but it does not directly study FRB/PRS, supernova engines, jets, neutrinos, or circumstellar interaction.
analysis.result: A CNN with $\mathcal{N}=10^{3}$ templates reaches a sensitivity distance comparable to SFT matched filtering, which instead needs approximately $\mathcal{N}_{\mathrm{SFT}}=10^{7}$ templates, about four orders of magnitude more. For $f_{\max}=10\,\mathrm{Hz}$ and $f_{\min}\in\{2,3,4,5\}\,\mathrm{Hz}$, the quoted evaluation time falls from minutes to milliseconds, a speed-up of about $1.6\times10^{4}$–$4.0\times10^{4}$; the CNN per-template cost is $\langle\mathfrak{c}_1\rangle\approx(3$–$25)\,\mu\mathrm{s}$. At fixed template number, sensitivity follows $\langle s\rangle\sim\rho_{\rm opt}^{2}(1-\langle\mu\rangle)$ with $\rho_{\rm opt}^{2}\propto\int_{f_{\min}}^{10\,\mathrm{Hz}}f^{-7/3}/S_n(f)\,df$.
analysis.problem: Early warning of binary neutron-star inspirals in third-generation detectors is limited by the computing cost of evaluating the detection statistic at low latency.
analysis.method: Early inspirals are represented by narrowband SFTs with $T_{\mathrm{SFT}}=31\,\mathrm{s}$ and $\Delta k=51$ bins about $f(t;\mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{c}})=f_{\max}[1+(256/5)(\pi f_{\max})^{8/3}(G\mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{c}}/c^{3})^{5/3}(t_{\max}-t)]^{-3/8}$. A CNN minimizes binary cross-entropy and searches only $\mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{c}}$, while the SFT statistic $\mathcal{X}$ is maximized analytically over phase and luminosity distance and then over an eight-dimensional bank. Latency is modeled as $\mathcal{C}=\mathcal{N}\langle\mathfrak{c}_1\rangle$, with $f_s=40\,\mathrm{Hz}$ for the 3, 4, and 5 Hz regimes.
limits: For lower chirp masses, evolution from $f_{\min}$ to $f_{\max}$ can exceed the fixed analysis window, so the signal is aligned at $f_{\max}$ and only its late portion is retained.

analysis.reason: This ZTF spectroscopic census of hydrogen-rich SLSNe directly constrains circumstellar interaction, pre-explosion mass loss, and possible Ia-CSM contamination, which are central to supernova-engine and CSM studies.
analysis.result: Of 106 hydrogen-rich SLSNe, 105 show narrow Balmer emission and are spectroscopically SLSNe-IIn; SN 2022lvm is the sole broad-lined SLSN-II in the discussed 2021–2022 subset comparison (1/36, 2.8%). Measured $L_{\mathrm{H}\alpha}$ spans $2.2\times10^{40}$ to $1.5\times10^{42}\,\mathrm{erg\,s^{-1}}$ (median $2.6\times10^{41}\,\mathrm{erg\,s^{-1}}$). The median Balmer decrement rises from 2.85 before $+100$ d to 4.40 afterward, below the Ia-CSM comparison medians 6.58 and 17.76. After excluding the SLSN-II and six Ia-CSM-like objects, median shell speed correlates with peak magnitude ($r=0.63$, $p=0.010$): brighter events tend to have lower $v_{\rm s}$. For 13 calibrated objects at $v_{\rm CSM}=100\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}}$ and $\epsilon=0.5$, $\dot{M}\sim0.028$–$0.30\,M_{\odot}\,\mathrm{yr^{-1}}$ from $L=\frac{1}{2}\epsilon\dot{M}v_{\rm s}^{3}/u_{\rm w}$. Six of 105 narrow-line events ($\sim6\%$) are Ia-CSM-like. Narrow interaction lines can persist beyond $+200$ d, with no Balmer morphology unique to SLSNe-IIn relative to fainter SNe IIn.
analysis.problem: Whether luminous narrow-line SLSNe-IIn are spectroscopically only the bright extreme of SNe IIn, what dense hydrogen-rich CSM and enhanced pre-explosion mass loss they require, and whether narrow Balmer lines plus high luminosity uniquely imply core collapse rather than Ia-CSM.
analysis.method: The study uses 304 optical spectra of 106 ZTF events selected at rest-frame peak $M\leq-19.9$ mag, with phases $(t-t_{\rm peak})/(1+z)$ and fluxes scaled by $10^{-0.4(m_{\rm GP}-m_{\rm syn})}$ from Gaussian-process light curves (287 absolutely calibrated). Balmer luminosity, pEW and FWHM are measured after local continuum subtraction. Single-epoch Monte Carlo electron-scattering snapshots (escatter; $10^{5}$ H$\alpha$ photons outside a cold dense shell) fit line profiles. Mass-loss rates use $L=\frac{1}{2}\epsilon\dot{M}\frac{v_{\rm s}^{3}}{u_{\rm w}}$ and $\dot{M}=\frac{2L}{\epsilon}\frac{u_{\rm w}}{v_{\rm s}^{3}}$, with luminosity integrated from the spectra and a blackbody extension to 3000–20000 Å.
assumptions: Quoted mass-loss rates use the adopted CSM-interaction model with $\epsilon=0.5$ and $v_{\rm CSM}=100\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}}$, commonly with a shock speed of $5000\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}}$.
limits: Inferred mass-loss rates are order-of-magnitude estimates rather than precise progenitor mass-loss histories.

analysis.problem: The work asks which progenitor mass is allowed by the nebular spectra of SN 1987A and whether the post-500 d optical deficit and UV behavior come from $\gamma$-ray leakage, molecular cooling, newly formed internal dust, or background-star contamination, rather than from circumstellar interaction.
analysis.method: One-dimensional, time-dependent NLTE radiative transfer with CMFGEN uses shuffled-shell macroscopic mixing and no microscopic mixing. The only power source is radioactive decay, dominated by the $^{56}\mathrm{Ni}$ chain, with nonlocal $\gamma$-ray deposition at gray opacity $\kappa_\gamma=0.06\,Y_e\,\mathrm{cm^{2}\,g^{-1}}$. Molecules are omitted in the global solution; a CO test retains only 10% of the C/O-shell absorbed decay power. After $\sim500\,\mathrm{d}$, $0.1\,\mu\mathrm{m}$ silicate dust is added only inside the metal-rich region at $v<2000\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}}$. Spectra are placed at $D=49.59\,\mathrm{kpc}$ with $E(B-V)=0.15\,\mathrm{mag}$, and model comparisons are normalized by absorbed decay power.
assumptions: The $^{56}$Ni decay chain dominates the radioactive power at all modeled epochs, and $^{56}$Ni bubbles and CSM interaction are omitted.
limits: Late-time metallicity variations have only a relatively weak spectral effect.

analysis.reason: This radiative Kerr-magnetosphere GRPIC study is useful for relativistic-jet launching and compact-object VHE emission because it quantifies current closure and gamma-ray output relative to the Blandford–Znajek power, but it is peripheral to FRB, pulsar-wind, and supernova-engine problems.
analysis.result: A polar spark gap and a variable equatorial current sheet jointly sustain the global poloidal current. With low pair multiplicity, synchrotron–curvature (SC) cooling leaves the overall structure largely unchanged but drives spark-gap electric-field oscillations; polar and equatorial variability have no significant cross-correlation and $\Delta t\sim l_{\rm rec}/(\mathcal{R}_{\rm in}c)\sim 10\,r_{\rm g}/c$ at $\mathcal{R}_{\rm in}\sim +0.1$. Post-processed bolometric luminosities are $L_{\rm IC}\sim 10^{-4}L_{\rm BZ}$ and $L_{\rm SC}\sim 10^{-2}L_{\rm BZ}$ (reported in the opening summary as SC up to $\sim 1\%$ and inverse Compton $\sim 0.1\%$ of the BZ luminosity), with spark-gap photons reaching sub-TeV energies. Balancing $t_{\rm SC}=6\pi m_{\rm e}c/(\sigma_{\rm T}f_{\perp,\rm eff}^{2}B_{0}^{2}\Gamma)$ and $t_{\rm acc}\approx\Gamma m_{\rm e}c/(ef_{D}B_{0})$ gives $\Gamma_{\rm max}=\sqrt{f_{D}/f_{\perp,\rm eff}^{2}}\,\Gamma_{\rm SC}\simeq 3.7\times 10^{6}$ for representative equatorial $B_{0}\sim 10^{2}\,\mathrm{G}$.
analysis.problem: The paper investigates how a polar spark gap and an equatorial current sheet jointly close the global poloidal current in a radiative, charge-starved Kerr black-hole magnetosphere, and how SC cooling changes particle acceleration, variability, and gamma-ray signatures relative to observed VHE flares.
analysis.method: The study uses axisymmetric 2D GRPIC in Kerr–Schild 3+1 form, evolving $\frac{1}{c}\partial_t\bm{B}=-\nabla\times\bm{E}$ and $\frac{1}{c}\partial_t\bm{D}=\nabla\times\bm{H}-\frac{4\pi}{c}\bm{J}$ with Hamiltonian particles, ambient-photon inverse Compton scattering, and two-photon pair creation. It compares no cooling, $\Gamma_{\rm SC}=\infty$, with marginal slow cooling, $\Gamma_{\rm SC}=800$, from a Wald vertical field at $a=0.99$, $\tilde{B}_{0}=5\times 10^{3}$, $\varepsilon_{0}=5\times 10^{-2}$, and $\tau_{0}=10$ ($\sigma_{0}\simeq 1.2\times 10^{4}$), followed by ray tracing. The SC drag is $\bm{g}\simeq-\frac{2}{3}\frac{e^{4}}{m_{\rm e}^{2}c^{4}}\Gamma^{2}\bm{\beta}B_{\perp,\rm eff}^{2}$.
assumptions: The adopted plasma supply has a low pair multiplicity, explicitly described as a low-pair-multiplicity parameter choice.
limits: Synthetic luminosity-variation amplitudes are smaller than the order-of-magnitude enhancements in prominent VHE flares.

analysis.research_progress: At low multiplicity, radiative cooling is an incremental correction to force-free current closure: the parabolic near-horizon geometry and global circuit persist, while pair-production efficiency causes gap oscillations. Both regions vary on $\Delta t\lesssim 10\,r_{\rm g}/c$, but only the polar region shows a distinct oscillation peak and their cross-correlation is insignificant. The radiative yields satisfy $L_{\rm SC}\sim 10^{-2}L_{\rm BZ}$ and $L_{\rm IC}\sim 10^{-4}L_{\rm BZ}$, with slow- and fast-cooling spectra $\Gamma dN/d\Gamma\propto\Gamma^{0}$ and $\propto\Gamma^{-1}$.

figures.caption: Figure 7: (a) Time- and volume-averaged particle spectra, $\overline{\Gamma\langle dN/d\Gamma/dV\rangle}$, during $t=219.93\sim 300.26\,r_{\rm g}/c$, for the polar-gap region ($r\leq 3.0\,r_{\rm g}$, $A_{\varphi}\leq A_{\varphi}(r_{\rm h},\pi/4)$). Solid (dashed) curves denote the msCl (nCl) model; blue (orange) curves represent electrons (positrons). (b,c) Temporal evolution of $\Gamma\langle dN/d\Gamma/dV\rangle$ at $\Gamma=\varepsilon_{0}^{-1}$ and the volume-averaged pair-production rate, $\langle\kappa_{\pm}\rangle$. (d–f) Same as (a–c), but for the equatorial current-sheet region ($r\leq 2.0\,r_{\rm g}$, $\theta\leq\pi/2$, $A_{\varphi}\geq A_{\varphi}(r_{\rm h},80^{\circ})$). In panels (a) and (d), green, blue, purple, and red arrows indicate $\Gamma=\varepsilon_{0}^{-1}$, $\Gamma_{\rm cool}$, $\Gamma_{\rm max}(B_{0})=\Gamma_{\rm SC}(f_{D}/f_{B_{\perp,\rm eff}}^{2})^{1/2}$ (Eq. ( 12 ), with $(f_{D},f_{B_{\perp,\rm eff}})=(10^{-1},10^{-1})$ for (a) and $(10^{-1},1.0)$ for (d)), and the time- and volume-averaged magnetization, $\sigma_{\pm}=B^{2}/4\pi n_{\pm}m_{\rm e}c^{2}$, respectively.
figures.label: Fig. 7
figures.physical_core: Time- and volume-averaged particle spectra and the evolution of $\Gamma\langle dN/d\Gamma/dV\rangle$ at $\Gamma=\varepsilon_0^{-1}$ and $\langle\kappa_{\pm}\rangle$ are compared for the polar spark gap and equatorial current sheet, with and without synchrotron-curvature cooling. Markers show $\Gamma_{\rm cool}$, $\Gamma_{\rm max}(B_0)$, and the magnetization $\sigma_{\pm}$; SC cooling truncates and oscillates the gap population, while the sheet spectrum is less sensitive to cooling.

figures.caption: Figure 10: (a) Time-averaged synthetic IC photon spectra during $t_{\rm obs}-r_{\rm obs}/c=220.0\sim 300.0\,r_{\rm g}/c$. figures.caption: Figure 7: Synthetic polarization images and quantitative polarization diagnostics produced by the reconnection-bubble model. Rows correspond to cases dominated by radial (top), azimuthal (middle), and vertical (bottom) magnetic perturbations, while all other parameters are kept fixed. From left to right, the columns show representative polarization maps at $t=0$, $5$, and $20$, the azimuthal polarized-intensity variation $\Delta I$, the azimuthal EVPA residual $\Delta{\rm EVPA}$, and the corresponding Stokes- $(Q,U)$ trajectories. The corresponding values of the memory coefficients $(f_{{\rm Mem},r},f_{{\rm Mem},\phi},f_{{\rm Mem},z},f_{{\rm Mem},\chi})$ are indicated in each panel. In all panels, the remaining parameters are fixed at $A_{0}=0.6$, $t_{\rm inj}=1$, $r_{\rm inj}=11$, $\tau_{\rm bubble}=12$, $\tau_{\rm Mem}=20$, and $f_{{\rm Mem},\chi}=0.3$. The observer inclination is fixed at a face-on configuration.
figures.label: Fig. 7
figures.physical_core: With spacetime, emission, and polarization transport fixed, component-dependent reconnection bubbles (mixing $\mathbf{B}=(1-w)\mathbf{B}_{0}+w\mathbf{B}_{\rm bubble}$) yield distinct horizon-scale signatures: radial memory drives inward EVPA shifts, azimuthal memory outward EVPA shifts, and vertical memory mainly suppresses polarized intensity, seen in $\Delta I$, $\Delta{\rm EVPA}$, and Stokes-$(Q,U)$ trajectories at $A_{0}=0.6$, $\tau_{\rm bubble}=12$, $\tau_{\rm Mem}=20$.

analysis.reason: Reports multi-band QPO detections and variability state transition in blazar relativistic jet, providing incremental constraints on jet instabilities and precession models.

analysis.problem: Origin of long-term radio and short-term optical QPOs together with changing variability states in the relativistic jet of BL Lac PKS 0754+100 at $z=0.266$.
analysis.method: Detrended light curves analyzed with GLSP and WWZ; significance via 100000 STINGRAY simulations of broken power-law PSD $P(f)$ under red-noise null hypothesis; trial factor $T=M\times S$ for global significance.

limits: sparse temporal sampling of the VLBA available observations and the strong dependence of brightness on viewing angle

figures.caption: Figure 4: Schematic illustration of the origin and development of QPOs. The X-ray emission originates in the innermost region of AGN and then propagates to the base of the relativistic jet, which produces the observed optical modulations. This optical modulation grows outwards towards the jets and affects the radio observations, which modifies the existing periodic modulation and also shows periodic modulation of a longer period.
figures.label: Fig. 4
figures.physical_core: Schematic of QPO propagation in the blazar jet: X-ray emission from the innermost AGN region reaches the jet base, producing the ~1.4-day optical modulation, which then grows outward and modifies the radio variability into a longer-period modulation.

figures.caption: Figure 1: SMMAN and TESS observations of PKS 0754+100: The black dots denote the flux density measurements with 1 $\sigma$ error bars. analysis.result: Stochastic acceleration appreciably changes the downstream particle spectrum whenever $\eta \gtrsim \xi_{\rm CR}$. For standard Model I parameters, including stochastic acceleration and wave feedback increases the gamma-ray flux between $\sim 1$ and $100\,\mathrm{GeV}$ by $\sim 50\%$. For an undamped $f(p)\propto p^{-4}$ Kolmogorov cascade, $P t_{\rm age}/P_{\rm CR}\approx (3/4)\eta/\xi_{\rm CR}$; acceleration times scale as $\tau_{\rm acc}\sim p^{1/3}$ (Kolmogorov) or $\sim p^{1/2}$ (Kraichnan), while source-free inertial spectra are $W\sim k^{-5/3}$ and $W\sim k^{-3/2}$. Upstream self-generated waves alone do not significantly modify the downstream spectrum because the cascade rapidly removes their energy.

analysis.method: The particle distribution and turbulent spectrum are evolved together through $\partial_t f=p^{-2}\partial_p(p^2 D_{pp}\partial_p f)$ and $\partial_t W+\partial_k F=-\Gamma W+S-D$, using quasi-linear $D_{pp}$, resonant damping $\Gamma$, and Kolmogorov or Kraichnan cascades. The SNR downstream is split into independent shells with adiabatic losses, and the $pp$ gamma-ray flux is integrated with Naima and Kafexhiu cross sections, comparing cases with and without stochastic acceleration and wave feedback.

analysis.research_progress: Beyond shock-only DSA, the calculation identifies $\eta \gtrsim \xi_{\rm CR}$ as the regime where downstream stochastic acceleration matters and finds a $\sim 50\%$ rise in the $1$--$100\,\mathrm{GeV}$ flux for Model I. analysis.reason: The paper is relevant to supernova and compact-merger neutrino transport because collisional flavor conversion need not settle to an attracting fixed point, and the resulting cycles or chaos shift time-averaged flavor populations. It is worth knowing rather than essential because it is a specialized kinetic bifurcation study, not a direct engine or high-energy observational constraint.
analysis.result: Homogeneous collective precession (HCP) is a rotating-frame fixed point, but it is not always attracting. As the electron collision rate $\kappa_e$ approaches $0.0025$ from below, the target growth rate and the HCP number offset vanish together (supercritical Hopf); near $\kappa_e\simeq0.018$ a finite-amplitude pair appears, and the unstable branch merges with the target near $\kappa_e\simeq0.0221$ (subcritical Hopf). An independent HCP crossing occurs at $\kappa_e\simeq0.0200194578$, before target destabilization at $\kappa_e\simeq0.0221481171$. For $0.034\le\kappa_e\le0.060$, successive maxima of $P_z$ period-double eight times toward a stable $256$-cycle, with spacing ratios approaching $\delta_{\rm F}\simeq4.669$. At $\kappa_e=0.055025$ the leading Lyapunov estimate is $\widehat\lambda_1\simeq2.8\times10^{-3}$ for bounded irregular evolution. The HCP balance is $s(u^\star)^2=z^\star\tau^\star$, while averages obey $s[\langle u\rangle_T^2+\mathrm{Var}_T(u)]=\langle z\rangle_T\langle Z\rangle_T+\mathrm{Cov}_T(z,Z)-\tfrac12\mathcal{B}_{u^2}$. The largest reported HCP-versus-time-average population deviation is $8.03\%$, set by the mean coherent torque rather than by stationarity.
analysis.problem: The issue is whether a collisionally balanced HCP state attracts neutrino flavor trajectories or whether collisional flavor instability instead produces Hopf cycles, period doubling, and chaos, and how far HCP or mean-only estimates miss the time-averaged flavor populations.
analysis.method: The full quantum kinetic equations are linearized in the rotating frame, including the response of the self-interaction field; after removal of the common phase, local attraction requires all seven Jacobian eigenvalues to have negative real parts. For energy-independent rates the collective matrix follows the monochromatic kinetics and residuals contract at least as $e^{-\kappa_* t}$. Root number is fixed by the sign of $\mathcal{C}$, and $\kappa_e$ is scanned with multiple shooting and Lyapunov estimates. Steady balance is $s(u^\star)^2=z^\star\tau^\star$, whereas the time-averaged identity keeps $\mathrm{Var}_T(u)$ and $\mathrm{Cov}_T(z,Z)$.

analysis.reason: The paper establishes an intrinsic hard X-ray point-source excess in the Nuclear Stellar Disk and associates it with high-mass white-dwarf intermediate polars and possibly millisecond pulsars, which is relevant compact-object high-energy context but not central to FRB, jet, neutrino, or supernova-engine studies.
analysis.result: Within the NSD ($|l|\lesssim 1.3^{\circ}$, $|b|\lesssim 0.3^{\circ}$), XMM-Newton finds a concentration of intrinsically hard point sources. Plane sources are softer, with mean $\mathrm{HR}\simeq 0.1$ (PN) and $\simeq-0.3$ (MOS), where $\mathrm{HR}\equiv(H-S)/(H+S)$, $H=4.5$–$12\,\mathrm{keV}$, and $S=2.0$–$4.5\,\mathrm{keV}$. Inside-versus-outside HR distributions differ at $>8\sigma$. At $-1.05^{\circ}<l<0.55^{\circ}$, observed $\mathrm{HR}\gtrsim 0.3$ exceeds $\mathrm{HR}<0.2$ predicted for $5\times10^{22}<N_{\rm H}<8\times10^{22}\,\mathrm{cm}^{-2}$. Hard and soft longitude/latitude distributions differ at $>12\sigma/9\sigma$ ($p=2\times10^{-35}/3\times10^{-20}$). Scale heights are $h_{l,\rm s}=2^{\circ}$ ($\sim280\,\mathrm{pc}$), $h_{b,\rm s}=0.31^{\circ}$ ($\sim44\,\mathrm{pc}$), $h_{l,\rm h}=0.66^{\circ}$ ($\sim90\,\mathrm{pc}$), and $h_{b,\rm h}=0.17^{\circ}$ ($\sim24\,\mathrm{pc}$). The stellar-mass distribution follows the soft sources better than the hard sources. The hard NSD population most likely consists of intermediate polars with high $M_{\rm WD}$, possibly plus MSPs; representative partial covering at $kT=36\,\mathrm{keV}$ gives $\mathrm{HR}\sim0.82$ versus $\sim0.36$ without it, and $\langle kT\rangle\approx34\,\mathrm{keV}$ for IPs versus $\approx11\,\mathrm{keV}$ for polars. The $\log N$–$\log S$ slope is $\alpha\sim1.35$–$1.5$.
analysis.problem: The paper tests whether the hard X-ray point-source concentration overlapping the NSD is an intrinsically harder compact-object population or only an artifact of large line-of-sight $N_{\rm H}$, and what that population implies for the unresolved sources underlying the Galactic-center and Galactic-ridge X-ray emission.
analysis.method: Using the XMM-Newton Heritage Survey and cleaned 4XMM-DR14 sources over $|l|<10^{\circ}$, $|b|<1^{\circ}$, the authors compare $\mathrm{HR}\equiv(H-S)/(H+S)$ inside and outside the NSD with count-rate and exposure-matched K–S tests. Because most sources lack reliable spectra, they simulate 274 parameter sets with XSPEC fakeit and EPIC-PN responses: $\mathrm{tbabs}\times\mathrm{powerlaw}$ for $\Gamma=0$–$3$ and absorbed APEC for $kT=1$–$36\,\mathrm{keV}$, spanning $N_{\rm H}=(1$–$30)\times10^{22}\,\mathrm{cm}^{-2}$ and $Z_{\rm Fe}=(0.5,1,2)Z_{\odot}$.

analysis.reason: IXPE polarization and spectral constraints on the Cyg X-1 corona’s aspect ratio and axial outflow are relevant to compact-object high-energy observations and jet-aligned geometry, but the work is peripheral to FRB, supernova-engine, and shock-breakout studies.
analysis.result: IXPE measures a 2–8 keV polarization of $(4.01\pm 0.20)\%$ parallel to the radio jet at inclination $27.51^\circ$, whereas static corona models give only $1$–$2.5\%$. Cylindrical outflow models with $h=H/(2R)\leq 0.8$ and $\beta_{\rm top}=0.5$–$0.9$ simultaneously give $\Gamma=1.6$ and $\sim 4\%$ polarization parallel to the symmetry axis; larger $h$ has $q_{\rm max}<4\%$ even at $\beta_{\rm top}=0.99$. Outflow suppresses radiative feedback as $f_\beta\propto(1-\beta)^2$. The discussion gives $\delta\approx 1.56$, $L\approx 0.3L_{\rm iso}$, $\ell=35.4(L_{\rm iso}/0.5\%L_{\rm Edd})(r_g/R)$, $t_{\rm IC}=0.03(R/r_g)R/c$, $B_{\rm eq}\approx 1.1\times 10^{7}(R/r_g)^{-1}\,\mathrm{G}$, $\sigma\approx 6.9(R/r_g)^{-1}$ and $v_A\approx 0.9c$, favoring a pair corona. The IXPE polarization-angle difference is $3.3^\circ\pm 3.2^\circ$; requiring the band-to-band Faraday difference to be $<0.11$ rad yields $\eta_\Delta<0.14(B_\parallel/10^{7}\,\mathrm{G})^{-1}$.
analysis.reading_entry: III Results - limits on the corona’s aspect ratio
analysis.problem: Static Comptonizing coronae underpredict the hard-state polarization of Cyg X-1: IXPE finds about $4\%$ polarization parallel to the radio jet, while static models give only $1$–$2.5\%$. The question is how small $h=H/(2R)$ must be and how fast an axial outflow must be to reproduce both $\Gamma=1.6$ and the polarization.
analysis.method: polrad-3D Monte Carlo polarized transfer is run in a three-dimensional cylinder with the symmetry axis along $z$, temporarily neglecting general relativity. Continuity gives $n(z)\propto\beta^{-1}$, with Thomson depths $t_z=\bar{n}\sigma_T H$ and $t_r=\bar{n}\sigma_T R$. Constant-$\beta$ and accelerating profiles from $\beta_0=0.1$ to $\beta_{\rm top}$ are compared for a $100\,\mathrm{keV}$ Maxwell–Jüttner plasma and unpolarized isotropic $10\,\mathrm{eV}$ cyclo-synchrotron seeds, using invariant optical depth and the full Klein–Nishina Fano matrix. Grids in $t_z$ and $\beta_{\rm top}$, with up to $6.4\times 10^8$ photons, are matched to $\Gamma=1.6$ and $q=4\%$ at $i=27.5^\circ$.
assumptions: The radial scale is taken to be $R\sim r_g$ because the flow is unlikely to concentrate the required energy into much smaller regions.
limits: Only $h\leq 0.8$ with $\beta_{\rm top}=0.5$–$0.9$ jointly fits $\Gamma=1.6$ and $4\%$ polarization; larger $h$ remains below $4\%$ even at $\beta_{\rm top}=0.99$.
citation_leads: The Shape and Velocity of Black Hole Coronas: “We find that models with $h\leq 0.8$ and $\beta_{\rm top}\,=\,0.5-0.9$ can give both”

IV Discussion: “Above we assumed that $R\sim r_{\rm g}$ as it seems unlikely that the flow can concentrate”
Appendix A Verification of the polrad-3D: “We verified the polrad-3D code by testing it against Chandrasekhar’s classical results”
analysis.research_progress: Relative to static models limited to $1$–$2.5\%$ polarization, a depth- or height-stratified outflow with feedback scaling $f_\beta\propto(1-\beta)^2$ reaches the observed $\sim 4\%$ polarization and $\Gamma=1.6$ for $h\leq 0.8$ and $\beta_{\rm top}=0.5$–$0.9$. The derived compactness and $v_A\approx 0.9c$ favor a compact, pair-dominated corona close to the black hole.

The polarization is given in terms of the normalized Stokes parameter $q=Q/I$, positive (negative) for the electric field polarization angle parallel (perpendicular) to the $z$ -axis. The dotted lines show results from interpolating the results from the original calculation grid. The solid lines and data points are from the final simulations. All results show models which give $\Gamma=1.6$.
figures.label: Fig. 1
figures.physical_core: Normalized Stokes parameter q=Q/I for coronas that produce photon index Γ=1.6, comparing constant-velocity outflows with plasmas accelerating linearly in depth from β0=0.1 to β_top; positive q means polarization parallel to the symmetry (jet) axis.

figures.caption: Figure 2: The top panel shows the highest polarization $q$ on the $\Gamma=1.6$ contour at a viewing inclination of 27.5 ∘ as a function of the aspect ratio of the corona in the stationary frame for outflows with constant $\beta$ (blue lines), $\beta$ linear in depth (red lines), and linear in height (green lines). For aspect ratios $h\leq 0.8$, we find solutions matching the observed $q=4$ %. The yellow band shows the observed value with a 0.5% systematic uncertainty band. The center and lower panels are only for the velocity stratified coronas. The center panel shows the $\beta_{\rm top}$ required to match the observed $q$ for $h\leq 0.8$, as well as the $\beta_{\rm top}$ -values giving the highest $q$ for h $\geq$ 1.6. The hatched regions show the values entering the yellow band of 4% $\pm$ 0.5%. The right $y$ -axis translates the $\beta_{\rm top}$ -values into the corresponding Lorentz factors. The lower panel shows the vertical (and for $h\geq 0.8$ the radial) depths of the models achieving $q\,=\,$ 4%, or, for models that fail, the depths that give the highest PD while $\Gamma\,=\,1.6$.
figures.label: Fig. 2
figures.physical_core: On the Γ=1.6 contour at inclination 27.5°, maximum q versus stationary-frame aspect ratio h for constant-β and velocity-stratified coronas; only h≤0.8 reaches the observed q≈4%±0.5%, requiring β_top≈0.5–0.9, with the corresponding vertical/radial depths.
